name: Otomo
hook: In 1925 a tiny air-cooled Otomo was the only Japanese car in a Tokyo race full of bigger foreign machines, and it came home second.
story:
Picture Tokyo in 1925. Most cars on the road are American. Fords come out of a plant in Yokohama. Chevrolets come out of Osaka.

Now a little Japanese car rolls up to a race. It is the Otomo. It is the only home-built car on the grid.

Its engine is about the size of a modern city car's. It is cooled by air, not water. The foreign cars around it have far more power.

The Otomo comes from Hakuyosha, a small Tokyo works. The man behind it is Junya Toyokawa. He was not a car man first. He made gyrocompasses for ships and aircraft.

The race starts. By the accounts that survive, the Otomo wins its heat. Then it takes second place against the big machines.

That same year two Otomos ship to Shanghai. They are the first Japanese cars ever sold abroad.

It could not last. About three hundred were built before the cheap American cars won the sales race. But for one afternoon, the little car held its own.
description: The Otomo was a light car built by Hakuyosha Ironworks in Tokyo from 1924 to about 1927, developed from engineer Junya Toyokawa's experimental Ales cars of 1921. It used an air-cooled four-cylinder engine of about 943 cc and came as a two- or four-seat tourer, a saloon or a van; a water-cooled model followed in 1926. It is counted as Japan's first mass-produced car and its first export, but locally assembled Fords and Chevrolets undercut it, and about 300 were built.
